content: Prolonged sedentary behavior is associated with increased risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and the development of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Evidence of low to moderate certainty suggests that spending more time in sedentary activities is linked to a higher risk of developing endometrial, colon, and lung cancers. The benefits of reducing sedentary behavior outweigh any potential risks. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that higher levels of sedentary behavior are linked to poorer health outcomes. It is recommended to minimize sedentary time to reduce health risks. However, due to variations in how sedentary behavior is assessed (e.g. Additionally, while patterns of sedentary behavior (e.g., frequency and duration of breaks) were reviewed, there is limited evidence to provide specific recommendations on these aspects. The relationship between sedentary behavior and health outcomes may vary depending on the type and domain of sedentary activity. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to determine how different types of sedentary behavior affect various health outcomes or how these associations may vary across subpopulations. Future studies employing harmonized reporting and methods that distinguish between different postures (e.g., lying, sitting, standing) will enhance understanding of sedentary behavior patterns. The interplay between sedentary behavior and physical activity levels has been investigated, with moderate certainty evidence showing that the relationship between sedentary behavior and all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, and cancer mortality varies by the amount of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity performed. Findings indicate that the negative effects of sedentary behavior are more pronounced in individuals with low levels of physical activity. Conversely, higher levels of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity can mitigate the adverse health outcomes associated with prolonged sedentary behavior. For example, engaging in 60–75 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity per day can attenuate or even eliminate the detrimental effects of sedentary behavior on health outcomes. For older adults (aged 65 years and older), physical activity provides numerous health benefits, including reduced all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, incident hypertension, site-specific cancers, type 2 diabetes, improved mental health (e.g., reduced anxiety and depression symptoms), cognitive health, and sleep quality. Physical activity also helps prevent falls, fall-related injuries, and declines in bone health and functional ability. It is strongly recommended that older adults engage in regular physical activity, including at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week, or an equivalent combination of both. Additionally, muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups should be performed on two or more days per week, and multicomponent physical activities emphasizing balance and strength training should be done on three or more days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. Older adults should aim to limit sedentary time and replace it with physical activity of any intensity, including light-intensity activities, to gain health benefits. For those engaging in high levels of sedentary behavior, exceeding the recommended levels of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity is advised to counteract the negative effects of prolonged inactivity. For pregnant and postpartum women, physical activity is associated with numerous maternal and fetal health benefits, including reduced risks of pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, excessive gestational weight gain, delivery complications, and postpartum depression. Physical activity during pregnancy does not increase the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, or delivery complications and is not associated with adverse effects on birth weight. Pregnant and postpartum women without contraindications should engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week, incorporating a variety of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities. Gentle stretching may also be beneficial. Women who were habitually active before pregnancy can continue their activities during pregnancy and postpartum. In summary, physical activity is beneficial across all life stages, including older adulthood and pregnancy, and can mitigate the adverse effects of sedentary behavior. While more research is needed to refine dose-response relationships and specific recommendations, the evidence strongly supports the promotion of regular physical activity and the reduction of sedentary time to improve health outcomes.
